summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework. French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply here as they do in the metropole. Same-sex relations were decriminalised in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the 1810 Code, though public morality provisions were subsequently used against LGBTQ people. No legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Legal gender recognition follows the simplified French procedure, available since 1 January 2017 under a law signed on 18 November 2016. Surgery and medical diagnosis are no longer required, and both self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were dropped from the final bill. A change of first name is handled at the registry office; a change of the gender marker still requires an appearance before a court. A 2017 bid to have the law recognise a 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation, so visitors whose papers carry a marker inconsistent with their presentation should expect documents to govern official handling.

Placement in places of deprivation of liberty follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not match gender presentation. Reporting from January 2018 indicates that in practice assignment weighs the person's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings. Against that, the national preventive-mechanism body issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across French places of detention, drawn from some 40 referrals since 2010; the opinion covers the French system applicable in Guadeloupe.

Protection machinery is in force. A conversion therapy ban published on 1 February 2022 carries two years' imprisonment and a fine of €30,000. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal with a maximum of €45,000 and/or 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Official figures released on 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018.

Support facilities exist on the island. Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities, and driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. During the opening, the visiting minister Aurore Bergé announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, including adapted structures for overseas territories.

Gender-affirming healthcare is legal in France domestically since 1979, and gender dysphoria was declassified as a mental illness by decree in 2010, a step French trans rights organisations said changed little beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains under ALD 31 with treatment funded by the Sécurité Sociale. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report documented significant problems in gender-affirming healthcare, citing lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, and recommending an informed-consent, self-determination model. The French Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem' and advised extreme caution on access, without that position changing actual practice.

Trans minors are a direct legislative target. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a group opposed to all gender transition for minors to report on youth gender care, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'; a bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no update since 23 July 2024, and prompted large-scale protests. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2.

Parentage following transition has been litigated. In 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be considered the mother of the child she conceived before her sex change. On surrogacy and foreign records, the Court of Cassation ruled on 5 July 2017 that a child born to a surrogate abroad can be adopted by the partner of the biological father, the Court of Appeal of Paris held in May 2019 that a Canadian birth certificate must be recognised, and in December 2019 the Court of Cassation ruled that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France.
tangentialFactors:
France's historical record on same-sex relations is uneven despite the 1791 and 1810 decriminalisation. Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942, later 331, set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual relations, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982, and the Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity under article 330, repealed in 1980. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980, which the Senate has yet to vote. In Alsace and Lorraine, annexed in 1940, men were interned in Nazi camps and persecuted under Vichy despite the absence of a sodomy law.

Free-speech limits drew objections when the 2004 law passed: civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders called it a serious infringement of free speech. The statute created the Haute autorité de lutte contre les discriminations et pour l'égalité, and Christian Vanneste, an MP from the ruling UMP party, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though that conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation.

Institutional turbulence around trans policy continued into 2022. It emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, the interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of the observatory commissioned to report on youth gender care; one member resigned and the president stepped away. In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks.

Blood donation deferrals for gay and bisexual men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022, a measure that bears on gay and bisexual men rather than on trans visitors as such. Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981 and drew 500,000 participants in 2019, with events in dozens of other cities; Guadeloupe's own community calendar is described below in resident-facing terms.
localsOnly:
Guadeloupe's community organisations have expanded their visible activity. An interview published on 6 September 2023 with Leïla of the group Secret's Out reported that community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, with activism described as advancing after sister island Martinique, and featured Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's. Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova announced on 21 March 2025 that they would partner on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025, described locally as a potential 'annus mirabilis' for the island's community.

The Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened 24 April 2024 as the first LGBT+ centre on the island, is run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations and provides reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities. Residents seeking care under ALD 31 are funded through the Sécurité Sociale, and the ILGA-Europe finding on inequitable access depending on location is a consideration for residents choosing where to seek gender-affirming treatment.

Education policy reaches residents directly. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms, and in February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage. The Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' in January 2019 to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline for students and staff, and requiring all French schools to give guidance on LGBTQ issues with 17 May as a special sensitisation day; in March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos had announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008-2009.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 25 May 2021 opinion of the national preventive-mechanism body reports on places of detention across France in general. The inventory does not source detention conditions specific to Guadeloupe's prisons, so the frequency and severity of the violations it describes on the island remains unresolved.

The compensation bill for men arrested under article 330 before 1980 passed the National Assembly in March 2024 but the Senate has yet to vote; the status of that bill after 23 July 2024, and of the Senate bill to ban medical transition under 18 after May 2024, are both unresolved in the sources. Whether the conversion therapy ban has been applied or prosecuted in Guadeloupe is not sourced.

Whether the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion provides trans-specific services, legal document assistance or interpretation is not stated in the inventory, and the composition of the federation of associations behind it is not enumerated. Likewise, the announced measures on gender-based violence for overseas territories are described only as announcements, with no sourcing on implementation, funding or timelines in Guadeloupe.

Entry and visa requirements, airport screening practices and any Guadeloupe-specific rules on identity documents for travellers were not covered by the source inventory and remain not sourced here.
